name: Willow bark
habitat: Wet ground — riverbanks, lake margins, ditches, damp thickets. Willows follow water, which makes them a landscape sign as well as a medicine.
identify: Long narrow leaves, usually with fine teeth, often paler or silvery underneath.
Slender flexible twigs that bend right around without snapping.
Buds are covered by a SINGLE cap-like scale — a reliable winter mark unique to willows.
Catkins in spring; bark bitter to taste.

lookalikes.name: Poplar and aspen
lookalikes.danger: Low — poplars are close relatives and carry the same salicylates, so a mix-up is not dangerous.
lookalikes.tell: Poplar leaves are broad and often triangular with flattened leaf stalks that make them tremble; buds have several scales, not one.

lookalikes.name: Oleander
lookalikes.danger: Lethal. Every part is highly cardiotoxic and a very small amount can kill.
lookalikes.tell: Oleander is an evergreen shrub of warm and Mediterranean climates with thick leathery leaves in whorls of three and showy pink or white flowers; willow leaves are thin, alternate, deciduous and its flowers are catkins. Oleander is a shrub of gardens and roadsides, not of wet riverbanks.

preparations.method: Simmer a small handful of scraped inner bark from young twigs in water for 15-20 minutes. It will be very bitter.
preparations.for_use: Pain and fever — the salicin it carries is the compound aspirin was derived from.

preparations.method: Chew the inner bark of a green twig.
preparations.for_use: Mild toothache and headache in the field.

preparations.method: Green willow rods, soaked and bent.
preparations.for_use: Basketry, frames, fish traps, shelter hoops.

cautions: It is aspirin's ancestor and carries aspirin's contraindications: anyone allergic to aspirin, anyone on anticoagulants, and anyone with a stomach ulcer or bleeding risk should avoid it.
NEVER give it to a child or teenager with a viral illness — the Reye's syndrome risk that applies to aspirin applies here.
The dose in a field decoction is uncontrolled and varies with species, season and how much bark you used.
It is a mild analgesic. It will not touch severe pain.
evidence: Salicin content is well established, and standardised willow bark extracts have been trialled for low back pain with modest positive results. A field decoction is far less predictable than those extracts.
